strings.name: Venus Williams
strings.summary: Venus Williams helped reshape women’s tennis with her serve, court coverage and attacking power, winning seven major singles titles and four Olympic golds. A long-time doubles partner of her sister Serena, she also became a prominent equal-prize-money advocate. She continued competing after Sjögren’s syndrome and injuries. After playing in Hong Kong in November 2026, she said she was considering her future week by week; she had not announced retirement.
strings.coverageNote: Selected verifiable milestones through November 16, 2026; not a live news archive.
strings.influence.rationale: Major and Olympic titles helped advance women’s tennis commercially and the equal-pay debate.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birthplace
strings.facts.f1.value: Lynwood, California, United States; raised in Compton.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Seven singles majors
strings.highlights.h1.text: Five Wimbledon and two US Open singles titles, alongside doubles success with Serena, established lasting influence.
strings.facts.f2.label: Education and early training
strings.facts.f2.value: Initially coached by parents Richard Williams and Oracene Price, then trained in Florida.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Olympics and equal prize money
strings.highlights.h2.text: Won one singles and three doubles Olympic golds and helped campaign for equal prize money at Wimbledon and other events.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Still competing in Hong Kong
strings.timeline.t1.text: Lost to Mary Stoiana in the first round, her 17th consecutive tour singles defeat; said she was proceeding week by week without a retirement decision.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Fourth Olympic gold
strings.timeline.t2.text: Won her third women’s doubles gold with Serena in London, bringing her personal Olympic gold total to four.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Health challenge disclosed
strings.timeline.t3.text: Revealed her Sjögren’s syndrome diagnosis and continued professional competition after adapting training and daily life.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Equal pay and Wimbledon title
strings.timeline.t4.text: Wimbledon introduced equal prize money after years of advocacy; she won her fourth singles title there that year.
strings.timeline.t5.title: First world No. 1 ranking
strings.timeline.t5.text: Reached the top of the WTA singles rankings, a significant milestone in Black women’s tennis history.
strings.timeline.t6.title: A breakthrough title year
strings.timeline.t6.text: Won her first Wimbledon and US Open singles titles plus singles and doubles golds at the Sydney Olympics.
strings.timeline.t7.title: First major singles final
strings.timeline.t7.text: Reached the US Open final at seventeen, establishing herself among the leading players.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Professional debut
strings.timeline.t8.text: Entered professional competition in Oakland at fourteen after years of family and youth training.
